Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on
$S^2$ ([[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]) and let $(Y_{lm})_{l\ge0,\ -l\le m\le l}$ be the
functions of [[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-associated-polynomial-normalization]] ([[def-complex-exponential]]).
Then $(Y_{lm})$ is a complete orthonormal family of the complex Hilbert space $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]):
the family is orthonormal, and if $F\in L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ satisfies
$\int_{S^2}F\overline{Y_{lm}}\,d\sigma=0$ for all $l\ge0$ and $-l\le m\le l$, then $F=0$ almost everywhere.
Consequently every $F$ has the expansion
$$F=\sum_{l=0}^\infty\sum_{m=-l}^{l}\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm},\qquad \|F\|^2=\sum_{l,m}|\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle|^2,$$
with $\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle=\int_{S^2}F\overline{Y_{lm}}\,d\sigma$ and finite-subset-net convergence
([[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]).

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

Then the following four assertions are equivalent:

1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$;
2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$;
3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$
   for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]);
4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$
   converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$.

Assertion 2 is the statement
$\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$
([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $k\in\mathbb N$. Finite componentwise sums and products of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$, and a composite of composable $C^k$ Euclidean maps is $C^k$. Scalar multiples are included among the finite componentwise operations. The assertions remain valid on an empty open domain.

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a$, then $D_vf(a)$ exists for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$ and equals $Df(a)v$. In particular $\partial_jf(a)=Df(a)e_j$, and the matrix of $Df(a)$ is $Jf(a)$.

Put $S=k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ with total-degree grading. A polynomial is homogeneous of degree $d$ if each occurring monomial has total degree $d$; $0$ is homogeneous in every degree. An ideal $J\subseteq S$ is homogeneous if $F=\sum_dF_d\in J$ implies $F_d\in J$ for every $d$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $P_l$ be the Legendre polynomials of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-legendre-rodrigues-equation]], and for $l\in\mathbb N$ and $0\le m\le l$ define the
function $w_{lm}:(-1,1)\to\mathbb R$ by

$$w_{lm}(t):=(-1)^m(1-t^2)^{m/2}\,\frac{d^m}{dt^m}P_l(t),$$

where $(1-t^2)^{1/2}>0$ denotes the nonnegative square root. Let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on
$S^2$ and let the angle coordinates be $\Phi(\theta,\varphi)=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\theta)$
([[lem-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-integral-in-angle-coordinates]],
[[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]). Then:

(a) each $w_{lm}$ extends continuously to $[-1,1]$, with $w_{lm}(\pm1)=0$ when $m\ge1$, and on $(-1,1)$
it satisfies the associated Legendre equation
$$-\bigl((1-t^2)w_{lm}'\bigr)'+\frac{m^2}{1-t^2}w_{lm}=l(l+1)w_{lm}\qquad(-1<t<1),$$
equivalently $(1-t^2)w_{lm}''-2tw_{lm}'+\Bigl[l(l+1)-\frac{m^2}{1-t^2}\Bigr]w_{lm}=0$;

(b) for fixed $m\ge0$ the functions $w_{lm}$, $l\ge m$, are pairwise orthogonal in $L^2((-1,1),dt)$:
$\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}w_{km}\,dt=0$ for $k\ne l$; moreover $0<\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}^2\,dt<+\infty$;

(c) with $b_{lm}:=\bigl(\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}^2\,dt\bigr)^{-1/2}>0$ and
$$Y_{lm}(\theta,\varphi):=b_{lm}\,w_{lm}(\cos\theta)\,\frac{e^{im\varphi}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\qquad(l\ge m\ge0),$$
extended by $Y_{l,-m}:=(-1)^m\overline{Y_{lm}}$ for $m\ge1$ (as functions of $(\theta,\varphi)\in(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)$,
$\overline{\ \cdot\ }$ denoting complex conjugation, [[def-complex-exponential]],
[[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]), one has $|Y_{l,-m}|=|Y_{lm}|$ and
$\overline{Y_{lm}}=(-1)^mY_{l,-m}$ for all $l$ and all $m$ with $|m|\le l$;

(d) the family $\{Y_{lm}:l\ge0,\ -l\le m\le l\}$ is orthonormal in $L^2(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$
([[def-inner-product-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]): for all $(l,m)\ne(l',m')$
with $|m|\le l$, $|m'|\le l'$, the integral $\int_{S^2}Y_{lm}\overline{Y_{l'm'}}\,d\sigma$ equals $0$, and it
equals $1$ when $(l,m)=(l',m')$;

(e) $w_{l0}=P_l$, and $w_{ll}(t)=(-1)^l\frac{(2l)!}{2^l l!}(1-t^2)^{l/2}$.

The functions $Y_{lm}$ are complex-valued $L^2$-functions on the sphere; no physical interpretation as angular
momentum eigenfunctions or spherical harmonics of an atom is asserted.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix a real parameter $\hbar>0$. Let
$(Y_{lm})_{l\ge0,-l\le m\le l}$ be the complete orthonormal family of $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ constructed in
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-associated-polynomial-normalization]] and
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-onb]], and let
$H:=\operatorname{span}\{Y_{lm}:-l\le m\le l,\ l\in\mathbb N\}$ be its algebraic (finite) span. Define operators
$A$ and $L_z$ on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ by the diagonal lemma
[[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]]:

$$D(A):=\Bigl\{F:\sum_{l,m}l^2(l+1)^2\,|\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad AF:=\sum_{l,m}l(l+1)\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm},$$
$$D(L_z):=\Bigl\{F:\sum_{l,m}m^2\,|\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad L_zF:=\sum_{l,m}\hbar m\,\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm},$$

the sums being in the Hilbert-space norm ([[def-hilbert-space]],
[[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). Finally, for $F$ in the finite span
$H$ and a chart point $(\theta,\varphi)\in(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)$ write $F(\theta,\varphi)$ for the value of $F$
at $\Phi(\theta,\varphi)$ and put

$$(\mathcal S F)(\theta,\varphi):=-\frac1{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta\bigl(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta F\bigr)(\theta,\varphi) -\frac1{\sin^2\theta}\partial_\varphi^2F(\theta,\varphi),\qquad (\mathcal D F)(\theta,\varphi):=-i\hbar\,\partial_\varphi F(\theta,\varphi),$$

where the partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Then:

(a) $A$ and $L_z$ are self-adjoint operators on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ with the displayed domains; on $Y_{lm}$ they
act by $AY_{lm}=l(l+1)Y_{lm}$ and $L_zY_{lm}=\hbar mY_{lm}$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]); $A$ is nonnegative, $\langle AF,F\rangle\ge0$, and
$A\mathbf 1=0$;

(b) $H$ is a core of $A$ and of $L_z$: the finite truncations
$F_N:=\sum_{l\le N}\sum_{m}\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm}$ of an element $F$ of $D(A)$ satisfy $F_N\to F$ and
$AF_N\to AF$ in $L^2$, and analogously with $L_z$;

(c) for every $F\in H$ and every chart point with $\sin\theta\ne0$,
$$\mathcal S F(\theta,\varphi)=(AF)(\theta,\varphi),\qquad \mathcal D F(\theta,\varphi)=(L_zF)(\theta,\varphi);$$

(d) for every $l$ the orthogonal projection $P_l$ of $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ onto the $(2l+1)$-dimensional span of
$Y_{l,-l},\dots,Y_{ll}$ reduces both $A$ and $L_z$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]), i.e. $P_lA\subseteq AP_l$
and $P_lL_z\subseteq L_zP_l$; consequently $A$ and $L_z$ commute on the finite span $H$, and for every $F\in D(A)$ with
$\sum_{l,m}\bigl(l(l+1)\hbar m\bigr)^2|\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle|^2<\infty$ one has
$AL_zF=L_zAF=\sum_{l,m}l(l+1)\hbar m\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm}$. Writing $c_{lm}=\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle$ and $\lambda_l=l(l+1)$, the maximal product domains are $D(AL_z)=\{F\in L^2:\sum_{l,m}(\lambda_l\hbar m)^2|c_{lm}|^2<\infty\}$ and $D(L_zA)=D(A)\cap D(AL_z)$. Thus this is exactly the common domain $D(AL_z)\cap D(L_zA)=D(L_zA)$, while the two maximal product domains need not coincide. The product-weight condition alone does not imply $F\in D(A)$: the vector with coefficients $c_{l0}=1/l$ for $l\ge1$ and all other coefficients zero belongs to $L^2$, has zero product weight, but does not belong to $D(A)$. The product-weight condition is not automatic for all $F\in D(A)\cap D(L_z)$.

The differential expression $\mathcal S$ is evaluated only away from the poles, where the coordinate formulas are
defined; no claim is made about a maximal differential operator on all of $S^2$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space. Vectors $x,y\in V$ are
**orthogonal**, written $x\perp y$, when

$$\langle x,y\rangle=0 .$$

For a subset $S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^\perp:=\{\,v\in V : \langle v,s\rangle=0 \text{ for every } s\in S\,\}.$$

**Orthogonality is symmetric.** If $\langle x,y\rangle=0$, then
$\langle y,x\rangle=\overline{\langle x,y\rangle}=0$, so $x\perp y$ exactly
when $y\perp x$; in particular the condition defining $S^\perp$ is symmetric in
its two arguments.

**$S^\perp$ is a linear subspace.** Let $s\in S$ and scalars $a,b$; then
$\langle 0,s\rangle=0$, and if $u,v\in S^\perp$ then
$\langle au+bv,s\rangle=a\langle u,s\rangle+b\langle v,s\rangle=0$ by linearity
in the first argument, so $au+bv\in S^\perp$. Thus $S^\perp$ is a linear
subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]) for every subset $S$, whether or not
$S$ is a subspace. Moreover $0\in S^\perp$ always, and $v\in V$ lies in
$\{0\}^\perp$ for every $v$, so $\{0\}^\perp=V$.

**Monotonicity.** If $S\subseteq T\subseteq V$, then every vector orthogonal to
all of $T$ is orthogonal to all of $S$, so $T^\perp\subseteq S^\perp$.

**Nontriviality of orthogonality.** By positive definiteness
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2=0$ exactly for $v=0$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]),
so a vector orthogonal to itself is zero, and $\{0\}^\perp=V$, $V^\perp=\{0\}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Use the notation of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-strongly-continuous-rotation-action]]: $S^2$, the polar measure $\sigma$ with
$\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$, the Hilbert space $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$, the complete orthonormal family $(Y_{lm})$, the blocks
$V_l$, the finite span $H$, the spaces $H_l^{\mathrm{pol}}$ of complex harmonic homogeneous polynomials of degree
$l$, the restriction maps $\mathrm{res}_l$, and the unitary action $U(R)F=\text{class of }\tilde F(R^{-1}\cdot)$
of $SO(3)$. Fix $\hbar>0$ and for $i=1,2,3$ define the rotation matrices
$$R_1(t):=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&\cos t&-\sin t\\0&\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix},\quad R_2(t):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&0&\sin t\\0&1&0\\-\sin t&0&\cos t\end{pmatrix},\quad R_3(t):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&-\sin t&0\\ \sin t&\cos t&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},$$
put $U_i(t):=U(R_i(t))$. Let $L_z$ denote the diagonal operator of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-laplacian-diagonal-domain]], set $S:=R_2(-\pi/2)$, $W:=R_1(\pi/2)$,
and define
$$L_3:=L_z,\qquad L_1:=U(S)^{-1}L_zU(S),\qquad L_2:=U(W)^{-1}L_zU(W),$$
with domains $D(L_1)=U(S)^{-1}D(L_z)$, $D(L_2)=U(W)^{-1}D(L_z)$ and $D(L_3)=D(L_z)$.
Here $e^{-itL_z/\hbar}$ is the explicit diagonal unitary sending $Y_{lm}$ to $e^{-itm}Y_{lm}$;
$e^{-itL_1/\hbar}$ and $e^{-itL_2/\hbar}$ mean its conjugates by $U(S)$ and $U(W)$, respectively.
The proof identifies these operators with the complete strong derivative generators, so this construction
has the same generator meaning without an appeal to an unrestricted spectral or Stone theorem. For a polynomial $p$ put
$$D_ip:=(x\times\nabla p)_i=\sum_{j,k=1}^3\varepsilon_{ijk}\,x_j\,\partial_kp,$$
where $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(1,2,3)\mapsto(i,j,k)$ and is $0$ when two indices
coincide. Then:

(a) each $L_i$ is a self-adjoint operator on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ with $U(R_i(t))=e^{-itL_i/\hbar}$ for all real
$t$; the finite span $H$ is contained in $D(L_i)$ and is a core of $L_i$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]);
and for $F\in V_l$ with polynomial representative $p_F\in H_l^{\mathrm{pol}}$ one has
$$L_iF=\mathrm{res}_l(-i\hbar\,D_ip_F),$$
that is, $(L_iF)(\Omega)=-i\hbar\,D_ip_F(\Omega)$ for $\sigma$-almost every $\Omega\in S^2$; in particular
$L_iY_{lm}\in V_l$ for all $l,m$ and $L_iH\subseteq H$;

(b) on $H$ the operators satisfy the commutation relations
$$L_iL_j-L_jL_i=i\hbar\sum_{k=1}^3\varepsilon_{ijk}L_k;$$

(c) $L_3=L_z$ as self-adjoint operators (equal domains and equal action); in particular $L_3Y_{lm}=\hbar mY_{lm}$, so that
$L_3$ is diagonal in the basis $(Y_{lm})$, and for every $F\in H$ and chart point $(\theta,\varphi)$ one has $(L_3F)(\theta,\varphi)=-i\hbar\,\partial_\varphi F(\theta,\varphi)$;

(d) rotational conjugation identifies the domains: with the two quarter-turn rotations
$S:=R_2(-\pi/2)$ and $W:=R_1(\pi/2)$ one has
$$U(S)L_1U(S)^{-1}=L_3,\qquad U(W)L_2U(W)^{-1}=L_3,$$
as self-adjoint operators, and consequently $U(S)D(L_1)=D(L_3)$ and $U(W)D(L_2)=D(L_3)$: the three domains
are unitarily identified.

All assertions are mathematical statements about operators on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$; no physical interpretation of
the generators as angular momentum is asserted, and no measurement postulate is used.

derivations.claim: [(a), the two harmonic pieces] By [F2] and $\Delta\mathcal H=0$, $\Delta(Q_q\mathcal H)=\sum_ic_{q,i}\Delta(x_i\mathcal H)=\sum_ic_{q,i}\,2\partial_i\mathcal H$. Since $\partial_i$ commutes with $\Delta$ and $\Delta\mathcal H=0$, each $\partial_i\mathcal H$ lies in $H_{l-1}^{\mathrm{pol}}$, so $G_q=\sum_ic_{q,i}\partial_i\mathcal H/(2l+1)\in H_{l-1}^{\mathrm{pol}}$; by [F2] and Euler's identity for the homogeneous polynomial $G_q$ of degree $l-1$, $\Delta(r^2G_q)=6G_q+4(l-1)G_q+r^2\Delta G_q=(4l+2)G_q+r^2\Delta G_q$, and here $\Delta G_q=0$, so $\Delta(r^2G_q)=(4l+2)G_q=2\sum_ic_{q,i}\partial_i\mathcal H$. Hence $\Delta R_q=\Delta(Q_q\mathcal H)-\Delta(r^2G_q)=0$: $R_q\in H_{l+1}^{\mathrm{pol}}$, and $R_q$ is homogeneous of degree $l+1$ as the difference of two such polynomials; for $l=0$ the derivative terms vanish because $\mathcal H$ is constant, so $G_q=0$ and $R_q=Q_q\mathcal H$.

[(b), degree selection] Restricting the identity of step 1.1 to $S^2$, where $r^2=1$, gives $Q_q|_{S^2}\cdot Y_{lm}=\mathrm{res}_{l+1}(R_q)+\mathrm{res}_{l-1}(G_q)$, where for $l=0$ the second term is omitted because $G_q=0$; for $l\ge1$ both restriction maps are the defined maps in [F1]. This is an element of $V_{l+1}+V_{l-1}$, using $\mathcal H|_{S^2}=Y_{lm}$ ([F1]) and $Q_q\mathcal H|_{S^2}=(Q_q|_{S^2})Y_{lm}$; the sum is direct and each summand lies in the corresponding block, so orthogonality $V_{l+1}\perp V_{l'}$ and $V_{l-1}\perp V_{l'}$ for $l'\notin\{l-1,l+1\}$ ([F1]) gives $\langle Q_q|_{S^2}Y_{lm},Y_{l'm'}\rangle=0$ for such $l'$.

[(c), weight selection] Let $F:=Q_q|_{S^2}\cdot Y_{lm}\in H$ by step 2.1. On the chart, by [F3] and [F4], $\partial_\varphi F=(\partial_\varphi Q_q)Y_{lm}+Q_q\,\partial_\varphi Y_{lm}=iq\,F+im\,F=i(m+q)F$; hence by [F5] $L_zF=-i\hbar\partial_\varphi F=\hbar(m+q)F$ in $H$. If now $m'\ne m+q$, then using the self-adjointness of $L_z$ ([F5]) and $L_zY_{l'm'}=\hbar m'Y_{l'm'}$, $\hbar(m+q)\langle F,Y_{l'm'}\rangle=\langle L_zF,Y_{l'm'}\rangle=\langle F,L_zY_{l'm'}\rangle=\hbar m'\langle F,Y_{l'm'}\rangle$, so $\langle F,Y_{l'm'}\rangle=0$.

[(d), the rules] Clause (d) restates steps 2.1 and 3.1 for the multiplier $Q_q$: a nonzero angular integral requires $l'\in\{l-1,l+1\}$ and $m'=m+q$; the case $l'=l-1$ presupposes $l\ge1$ because $-l'\le m'\le l'$ with $l-1\ge0$; and by [F6] the weight $m$ is the $L_3$-eigenvalue in units $\hbar$, so the multiplier $Q_q$ shifts the $L_3$-eigenvalue by $\hbar q$.

Let $s\in\frac12\mathbb N=\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $N:=2s\in\mathbb N$ and let
$V_s:=\mathbb C^{N+1}$ carry the standard inner product
$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_k\overline{w_k}$, linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Write $(e_m)_{-s\le m\le s}$ for the standard basis, indexed so that
$e_m$ is the vector with entry $1$ in position $k=s-m$ and entry $0$ elsewhere; thus
$\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=1$ if $m=n$ and $\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=0$ otherwise. Define $\mathbb C$-linear maps
$J_z,J_+,J_-\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_s)$ by their values on this basis ([[def-linear-map]]):

$$J_ze_m:=m\,e_m,\qquad J_+e_m:=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}\,e_{m+1},\qquad J_-e_m:=\sqrt{(s+m)(s-m+1)}\,e_{m-1},$$

where $e_{s+1}:=0$ and $e_{-s-1}:=0$, and put

$$J_x:=\tfrac12(J_++J_-),\qquad J_y:=\tfrac1{2i}(J_+-J_-),\qquad J^2:=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2 .$$

Then:

(a) $J_z$, $J_x$ and $J_y$ are self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V_s$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]);

(b) on $V_s$ the commutators are

$$[J_z,J_+]=J_+,\qquad [J_z,J_-]=-J_-,\qquad [J_+,J_-]=2J_z,\qquad [J_x,J_y]=iJ_z,\qquad [J_y,J_z]=iJ_x,\qquad [J_z,J_x]=iJ_y ;$$

(c) $J^2=J_-J_++J_z^2+J_z=J_+J_-+J_z^2-J_z=s(s+1)I$, and $[J^2,J_z]=[J^2,J_\pm]=0$;

(d) the matrix elements of the raising operator are
$\|J_+e_m\|^2=(s-m)(s+m+1)$ and $\|J_-e_m\|^2=(s+m)(s-m+1)$, and

derivations.claim: [(a), the nine pairings] By [F2], $\|\Psi\|^2=(\|e_+\otimes e_-\|^2+\|e_-\otimes e_+\|^2)/2=1$. (e) for each $j\in\{|s-t|,\dots,s+t\}$ the space of vectors of $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_z$-eigenvalue $j$ orthogonal to
all summands $W_{j'}$ with $j'>j$ is one-dimensional; for a unit vector $u_j$ in it the vectors
$$v_{j,k}:=\bigl(k!(2j)(2j-1)\cdots(2j-k+1)\bigr)^{-1/2}(J^{\mathrm{tot}}_-)^ku_j\qquad(0\le k\le2j)$$
form an orthonormal basis of $W_j$ with $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_zv_{j,k}=(j-k)v_{j,k}$,
$J^{\mathrm{tot}}_+v_{j,k}=\sqrt{k(2j-k+1)}\,v_{j,k-1}$ and
$J^{\mathrm{tot}}_-v_{j,k}=\sqrt{(k+1)(2j-k)}\,v_{j,k+1}$; the coefficients of $v_{j,k}$ in the product basis
are therefore determined by the phase of $u_j$, and choosing that phase fixes the Clebsch-Gordan numbers
explicitly; in particular $u_{s+t}=e^{(s)}_s\otimes e^{(t)}_t$ is a permissible choice.

The theorem is a purely mathematical statement about tensor products of the explicit matrices of
[[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]]; it asserts no physical coupling, conservation law or
measurement fact.

derivations.claim: [(a) orthonormality] By [F2], $\langle w_{1,1},w_{1,0}\rangle=(\langle e_+,e_+\rangle\langle e_+,e_-\rangle+\langle e_+,e_-\rangle\langle e_+,e_+\rangle)/\sqrt2=0$, and similarly for all pairs: the tensors $e_+\otimes e_+$, $e_-\otimes e_-$, $(e_+\otimes e_-+e_-\otimes e_+)/\sqrt2$ and $(e_+\otimes e_--e_-\otimes e_+)/\sqrt2$ are mutually orthogonal of norm $1$ because the four tensors $e_\pm\otimes e_\pm$ are orthonormal and the two combined vectors are orthogonal to them and to each other. Since $\dim(V\widehat\otimes V)=4$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]), these four vectors form an orthonormal basis.

[(b) triplet] By [F1] and [F3]: $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_zw_{1,1}=(J^{(1/2)}_ze_+)\otimes e_++e_+\otimes(J^{(1/2)}_ze_+)=\tfrac12w_{1,1}+\tfrac12w_{1,1}=w_{1,1}$; $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_z(e_+\otimes e_-)=(\tfrac12-\tfrac12)e_+\otimes e_-=0$ and $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_z(e_-\otimes e_+)=(-\tfrac12+\tfrac12)e_-\otimes e_+=0$, so $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_zw_{1,0}=0$; and $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_zw_{1,-1}=-w_{1,-1}$. Moreover $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_+w_{1,1}=0$ (both terms vanish by [F1]), so $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_-J^{\mathrm{tot}}_+w_{1,1}=0$; hence $J^{\mathrm{tot}\,2}w_{1,1}=(0+1^2+1)w_{1,1}=2w_{1,1}$ by [F3].

[(b) singlet] $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_zw_{0,0}=\bigl(\tfrac12e_+\otimes e_-+\tfrac12e_-\otimes e_+-\tfrac12e_+\otimes e_- - \tfrac12e_-\otimes e_+\bigr)/\sqrt2=0$; moreover $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_+w_{0,0}=\bigl(J^{(1/2)}_+e_+\otimes e_-+e_+\otimes J^{(1/2)}_+e_- - J^{(1/2)}_+e_-\otimes e_+ - e_-\otimes J^{(1/2)}_+e_+\bigr)/\sqrt2=(0+e_+\otimes e_+ - e_+\otimes e_+ -0)/\sqrt2=0$ and $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_-w_{0,0}=\bigl(J^{(1/2)}_-e_+\otimes e_-+e_+\otimes J^{(1/2)}_-e_- - J^{(1/2)}_-e_-\otimes e_+ - e_-\otimes J^{(1/2)}_-e_+\bigr)/\sqrt2=(e_-\otimes e_-+0-0-e_-\otimes e_-)/\sqrt2=0$ by [F1] and [F3]. Hence $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_iw_{0,0}=0$ for all $i$, since $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_x=\tfrac12(J^{\mathrm{tot}}_++J^{\mathrm{tot}}_-)$ and $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_y=\tfrac1{2i}(J^{\mathrm{tot}}_+-J^{\mathrm{tot}}_-)$, and consequently $J^{\mathrm{tot}\,2}w_{0,0}=0$.

[(c) ladder] Using [F1] and [F3]: $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_+w_{1,1}=(J^{(1/2)}_+e_+)\otimes e_++e_+\otimes(J^{(1/2)}_+e_+)=0$; $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_+w_{1,0}=[(J^{(1/2)}_+e_+)\otimes e_-+e_+\otimes(J^{(1/2)}_+e_-)+(J^{(1/2)}_+e_-)\otimes e_++e_-\otimes(J^{(1/2)}_+e_+)]/\sqrt2=(0+e_+\otimes e_++e_+\otimes e_++0)/\sqrt2=\sqrt2\,w_{1,1}$; and $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_+w_{1,-1}=(J^{(1/2)}_+e_-)\otimes e_-+e_-\otimes(J^{(1/2)}_+e_-)=e_+\otimes e_-+e_-\otimes e_+=\sqrt2\,w_{1,0}$. Since $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_-=(J^{\mathrm{tot}}_+)^*$ ([F1] self-adjointness and [F3]), the adjoint relations follow: $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_-w_{1,-1}=0$, $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_-w_{1,0}=\sqrt2w_{1,-1}$, $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_-w_{1,1}=\sqrt2w_{1,0}$ (each verified by pairing with the orthonormal basis vectors of step 1.1). Together with step 1.2 this shows that sending $e_m\mapsto w_{1,m}$ carries the spin-$1$ operators of [[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]] to $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_x,J^{\mathrm{tot}}_y,J^{\mathrm{tot}}_z$ on the triplet: the spin-$1$ model has $J_+e_0=\sqrt2e_1$, $J_+e_{-1}=\sqrt2e_0$, $J_+e_1=0$ and $J_ze_m=m e_m$, matching steps 1.2 and this step, and $J_x,J_y$ are recovered from $J_\pm$; the singlet span is orthogonal to the triplet by step 1.1 and is annihilated by all $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_i$ by step 1.3, so this is exactly the decomposition of [F4] for $s=t=\tfrac12$.

boundaries.evidence: The case of the zero vector is covered by linearity; every displayed vector is verified nonzero with norm one in step 1.1 (example, clause (a)).
The singlet solves J^tot_i w=0 for all i, which is the zero-eigenvalue clause (example, clause (b), step 1.3).
The highest-weight vector w_{1,1} and the unit normalization of all four basis vectors are the one-cases (example, clauses (a),(b)).
The J^tot_z-eigenvalue 0 is two-dimensional, spanned by w_{1,0} and w_{0,0}, and the example displays both (example, clauses (b),(a)).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Use the notation of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-strongly-continuous-rotation-action]]: $S^2$, the polar measure $\sigma$ with
$\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$, the Hilbert space $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$, the complete orthonormal family $(Y_{lm})$, the blocks
$V_l$, the finite span $H$, the spaces $H_l^{\mathrm{pol}}$ of complex harmonic homogeneous polynomials of degree
$l$, the restriction maps $\mathrm{res}_l$, and the unitary action $U(R)F=\text{class of }\tilde F(R^{-1}\cdot)$
of $SO(3)$. Fix $\hbar>0$ and for $i=1,2,3$ define the rotation matrices
$$R_1(t):=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&\cos t&-\sin t\\0&\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix},\quad R_2(t):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&0&\sin t\\0&1&0\\-\sin t&0&\cos t\end{pmatrix},\quad R_3(t):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&-\sin t&0\\ \sin t&\cos t&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},$$
put $U_i(t):=U(R_i(t))$. Let $L_z$ denote the diagonal operator of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-laplacian-diagonal-domain]], set $S:=R_2(-\pi/2)$, $W:=R_1(\pi/2)$,
and define
$$L_3:=L_z,\qquad L_1:=U(S)^{-1}L_zU(S),\qquad L_2:=U(W)^{-1}L_zU(W),$$
with domains $D(L_1)=U(S)^{-1}D(L_z)$, $D(L_2)=U(W)^{-1}D(L_z)$ and $D(L_3)=D(L_z)$.
Here $e^{-itL_z/\hbar}$ is the explicit diagonal unitary sending $Y_{lm}$ to $e^{-itm}Y_{lm}$;
$e^{-itL_1/\hbar}$ and $e^{-itL_2/\hbar}$ mean its conjugates by $U(S)$ and $U(W)$, respectively.
The proof identifies these operators with the complete strong derivative generators, so this construction
has the same generator meaning without an appeal to an unrestricted spectral or Stone theorem. For a polynomial $p$ put
$$D_ip:=(x\times\nabla p)_i=\sum_{j,k=1}^3\varepsilon_{ijk}\,x_j\,\partial_kp,$$
where $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(1,2,3)\mapsto(i,j,k)$ and is $0$ when two indices
coincide. Then:

(a) each $L_i$ is a self-adjoint operator on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ with $U(R_i(t))=e^{-itL_i/\hbar}$ for all real
$t$; the finite span $H$ is contained in $D(L_i)$ and is a core of $L_i$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]);
and for $F\in V_l$ with polynomial representative $p_F\in H_l^{\mathrm{pol}}$ one has
$$L_iF=\mathrm{res}_l(-i\hbar\,D_ip_F),$$
that is, $(L_iF)(\Omega)=-i\hbar\,D_ip_F(\Omega)$ for $\sigma$-almost every $\Omega\in S^2$; in particular
$L_iY_{lm}\in V_l$ for all $l,m$ and $L_iH\subseteq H$;

(b) on $H$ the operators satisfy the commutation relations
$$L_iL_j-L_jL_i=i\hbar\sum_{k=1}^3\varepsilon_{ijk}L_k;$$

(c) $L_3=L_z$ as self-adjoint operators (equal domains and equal action); in particular $L_3Y_{lm}=\hbar mY_{lm}$, so that
$L_3$ is diagonal in the basis $(Y_{lm})$, and for every $F\in H$ and chart point $(\theta,\varphi)$ one has $(L_3F)(\theta,\varphi)=-i\hbar\,\partial_\varphi F(\theta,\varphi)$;

(d) rotational conjugation identifies the domains: with the two quarter-turn rotations
$S:=R_2(-\pi/2)$ and $W:=R_1(\pi/2)$ one has
$$U(S)L_1U(S)^{-1}=L_3,\qquad U(W)L_2U(W)^{-1}=L_3,$$
as self-adjoint operators, and consequently $U(S)D(L_1)=D(L_3)$ and $U(W)D(L_2)=D(L_3)$: the three domains
are unitarily identified.

All assertions are mathematical statements about operators on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$; no physical interpretation of
the generators as angular momentum is asserted, and no measurement postulate is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$S^2:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ and let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on $S^2$ of
[[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], a finite Borel measure ([[def-measure]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Let

$$\Phi:(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)\to S^2,\qquad \Phi(\theta,\varphi):=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta),$$

and let $H:=\{(x,y,0)\in\mathbb R^3:x\ge0\}$ denote the closed half-plane, a Lebesgue-null Borel set
([[thm-affine-hyperplanes-and-proper-subspaces-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]]). Then:

(a) for every Borel function $F:S^2\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int_{S^2}F\,d\sigma=\int_{(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)}F\bigl(\Phi(\theta,\varphi)\bigr)\,\sin\theta\ d(\theta,\varphi),$$
the right-hand integral being the Lebesgue integral over the open rectangle;

(b) $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$;

(c) the identity of (a) holds with $F\in L^1(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$ in the sense that $F\circ\Phi$ is Lebesgue
integrable on the rectangle against $\sin\theta\,d(\theta,\varphi)$ and the two integrals agree (real and
imaginary parts, positive and negative parts).

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $P_l$ be the Legendre polynomials of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-legendre-rodrigues-equation]], and for $l\in\mathbb N$ and $0\le m\le l$ define the
function $w_{lm}:(-1,1)\to\mathbb R$ by

$$w_{lm}(t):=(-1)^m(1-t^2)^{m/2}\,\frac{d^m}{dt^m}P_l(t),$$

where $(1-t^2)^{1/2}>0$ denotes the nonnegative square root. Let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on
$S^2$ and let the angle coordinates be $\Phi(\theta,\varphi)=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\theta)$
([[lem-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-integral-in-angle-coordinates]],
[[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]). Then:

(a) each $w_{lm}$ extends continuously to $[-1,1]$, with $w_{lm}(\pm1)=0$ when $m\ge1$, and on $(-1,1)$
it satisfies the associated Legendre equation
$$-\bigl((1-t^2)w_{lm}'\bigr)'+\frac{m^2}{1-t^2}w_{lm}=l(l+1)w_{lm}\qquad(-1<t<1),$$
equivalently $(1-t^2)w_{lm}''-2tw_{lm}'+\Bigl[l(l+1)-\frac{m^2}{1-t^2}\Bigr]w_{lm}=0$;

(b) for fixed $m\ge0$ the functions $w_{lm}$, $l\ge m$, are pairwise orthogonal in $L^2((-1,1),dt)$:
$\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}w_{km}\,dt=0$ for $k\ne l$; moreover $0<\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}^2\,dt<+\infty$;

(c) with $b_{lm}:=\bigl(\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}^2\,dt\bigr)^{-1/2}>0$ and
$$Y_{lm}(\theta,\varphi):=b_{lm}\,w_{lm}(\cos\theta)\,\frac{e^{im\varphi}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\qquad(l\ge m\ge0),$$
extended by $Y_{l,-m}:=(-1)^m\overline{Y_{lm}}$ for $m\ge1$ (as functions of $(\theta,\varphi)\in(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)$,
$\overline{\ \cdot\ }$ denoting complex conjugation, [[def-complex-exponential]],
[[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]), one has $|Y_{l,-m}|=|Y_{lm}|$ and
$\overline{Y_{lm}}=(-1)^mY_{l,-m}$ for all $l$ and all $m$ with $|m|\le l$;

(d) the family $\{Y_{lm}:l\ge0,\ -l\le m\le l\}$ is orthonormal in $L^2(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$
([[def-inner-product-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]): for all $(l,m)\ne(l',m')$
with $|m|\le l$, $|m'|\le l'$, the integral $\int_{S^2}Y_{lm}\overline{Y_{l'm'}}\,d\sigma$ equals $0$, and it
equals $1$ when $(l,m)=(l',m')$;

(e) $w_{l0}=P_l$, and $w_{ll}(t)=(-1)^l\frac{(2l)!}{2^l l!}(1-t^2)^{l/2}$.

The functions $Y_{lm}$ are complex-valued $L^2$-functions on the sphere; no physical interpretation as angular
momentum eigenfunctions or spherical harmonics of an atom is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix a real parameter $\hbar>0$. Let
$(Y_{lm})_{l\ge0,-l\le m\le l}$ be the complete orthonormal family of $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ constructed in
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-associated-polynomial-normalization]] and
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-onb]], and let
$H:=\operatorname{span}\{Y_{lm}:-l\le m\le l,\ l\in\mathbb N\}$ be its algebraic (finite) span. Define operators
$A$ and $L_z$ on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ by the diagonal lemma
[[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]]:

$$D(A):=\Bigl\{F:\sum_{l,m}l^2(l+1)^2\,|\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad AF:=\sum_{l,m}l(l+1)\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm},$$
$$D(L_z):=\Bigl\{F:\sum_{l,m}m^2\,|\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad L_zF:=\sum_{l,m}\hbar m\,\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm},$$

the sums being in the Hilbert-space norm ([[def-hilbert-space]],
[[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). Finally, for $F$ in the finite span
$H$ and a chart point $(\theta,\varphi)\in(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)$ write $F(\theta,\varphi)$ for the value of $F$
at $\Phi(\theta,\varphi)$ and put

$$(\mathcal S F)(\theta,\varphi):=-\frac1{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta\bigl(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta F\bigr)(\theta,\varphi) -\frac1{\sin^2\theta}\partial_\varphi^2F(\theta,\varphi),\qquad (\mathcal D F)(\theta,\varphi):=-i\hbar\,\partial_\varphi F(\theta,\varphi),$$

where the partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Then:

(a) $A$ and $L_z$ are self-adjoint operators on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ with the displayed domains; on $Y_{lm}$ they
act by $AY_{lm}=l(l+1)Y_{lm}$ and $L_zY_{lm}=\hbar mY_{lm}$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]); $A$ is nonnegative, $\langle AF,F\rangle\ge0$, and
$A\mathbf 1=0$;

(b) $H$ is a core of $A$ and of $L_z$: the finite truncations
$F_N:=\sum_{l\le N}\sum_{m}\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm}$ of an element $F$ of $D(A)$ satisfy $F_N\to F$ and
$AF_N\to AF$ in $L^2$, and analogously with $L_z$;

(c) for every $F\in H$ and every chart point with $\sin\theta\ne0$,
$$\mathcal S F(\theta,\varphi)=(AF)(\theta,\varphi),\qquad \mathcal D F(\theta,\varphi)=(L_zF)(\theta,\varphi);$$

(d) for every $l$ the orthogonal projection $P_l$ of $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ onto the $(2l+1)$-dimensional span of
$Y_{l,-l},\dots,Y_{ll}$ reduces both $A$ and $L_z$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]), i.e. $P_lA\subseteq AP_l$
and $P_lL_z\subseteq L_zP_l$; consequently $A$ and $L_z$ commute on the finite span $H$, and for every $F\in D(A)$ with
$\sum_{l,m}\bigl(l(l+1)\hbar m\bigr)^2|\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle|^2<\infty$ one has
$AL_zF=L_zAF=\sum_{l,m}l(l+1)\hbar m\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm}$. Writing $c_{lm}=\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle$ and $\lambda_l=l(l+1)$, the maximal product domains are $D(AL_z)=\{F\in L^2:\sum_{l,m}(\lambda_l\hbar m)^2|c_{lm}|^2<\infty\}$ and $D(L_zA)=D(A)\cap D(AL_z)$. Thus this is exactly the common domain $D(AL_z)\cap D(L_zA)=D(L_zA)$, while the two maximal product domains need not coincide. The product-weight condition alone does not imply $F\in D(A)$: the vector with coefficients $c_{l0}=1/l$ for $l\ge1$ and all other coefficients zero belongs to $L^2$, has zero product weight, but does not belong to $D(A)$. The product-weight condition is not automatic for all $F\in D(A)\cap D(L_z)$.

The differential expression $\mathcal S$ is evaluated only away from the poles, where the coordinate formulas are
defined; no claim is made about a maximal differential operator on all of $S^2$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

Let $s\in\frac12\mathbb N=\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $N:=2s\in\mathbb N$ and let
$V_s:=\mathbb C^{N+1}$ carry the standard inner product
$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_k\overline{w_k}$, linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Write $(e_m)_{-s\le m\le s}$ for the standard basis, indexed so that
$e_m$ is the vector with entry $1$ in position $k=s-m$ and entry $0$ elsewhere; thus
$\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=1$ if $m=n$ and $\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=0$ otherwise. Define $\mathbb C$-linear maps
$J_z,J_+,J_-\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_s)$ by their values on this basis ([[def-linear-map]]):

$$J_ze_m:=m\,e_m,\qquad J_+e_m:=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}\,e_{m+1},\qquad J_-e_m:=\sqrt{(s+m)(s-m+1)}\,e_{m-1},$$

where $e_{s+1}:=0$ and $e_{-s-1}:=0$, and put

$$J_x:=\tfrac12(J_++J_-),\qquad J_y:=\tfrac1{2i}(J_+-J_-),\qquad J^2:=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2 .$$

Then:

(a) $J_z$, $J_x$ and $J_y$ are self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V_s$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]);

(b) on $V_s$ the commutators are

$$[J_z,J_+]=J_+,\qquad [J_z,J_-]=-J_-,\qquad [J_+,J_-]=2J_z,\qquad [J_x,J_y]=iJ_z,\qquad [J_y,J_z]=iJ_x,\qquad [J_z,J_x]=iJ_y ;$$

(c) $J^2=J_-J_++J_z^2+J_z=J_+J_-+J_z^2-J_z=s(s+1)I$, and $[J^2,J_z]=[J^2,J_\pm]=0$;

(d) the matrix elements of the raising operator are
$\|J_+e_m\|^2=(s-m)(s+m+1)$ and $\|J_-e_m\|^2=(s+m)(s-m+1)$, and
$\langle J_+e_m,e_{m+1}\rangle=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}$, which is nonzero exactly when $m<s$;

(e) for $s=\tfrac12$, identify $V_{\frac12}=\mathbb C^2$ with the basis ordered as $(e_{\frac12},e_{-\frac12})$ and let

$$\sigma_x:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$

be the Pauli matrices. Then $J_i=\tfrac12\sigma_i$ for $i=x,y,z$, $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_y^2=\sigma_z^2=I$,
$\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$, and consequently
$\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=2\delta_{ij}I$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\sum_k\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$ for all $i,j$, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ denotes the sign of the permutation $(x,y,z)\mapsto(i,j,k)$.

All statements are finite-dimensional linear algebra: no physical interpretation of $J_x,J_y,J_z$ as angular momentum, and no measurement postulate, is asserted here.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space with induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. Then $\|v\|\ge0$ with $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $\lambda$, and $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$; hence $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm on $V$, read over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]].

derivations.claim: [(a) orthonormality and identification] By [F2], $\|v_0\|^2=d^2\tfrac{4\pi}3=1$, $\|v_{\pm1}\|^2=\tfrac{d^2}2(\tfrac{4\pi}3+\tfrac{4\pi}3)=1$, and $\langle v_1,v_0\rangle=\langle v_1,v_{-1}\rangle=\langle v_0,v_{-1}\rangle=0$; so the $v_m$ are orthonormal, and since $\dim V_1=3$ they form an orthonormal basis of $V_1$ ([F4]). Comparing with the displayed values of [F3]: $Y_{1,0}=d\Omega_3=v_0$, $Y_{1,1}=-\sqrt{3/(8\pi)}(\Omega_1+i\Omega_2)=-\tfrac{d}{\sqrt2}(\Omega_1+i\Omega_2)=v_1$ (because $\sqrt{3/(8\pi)}=d/\sqrt2$), and $Y_{1,-1}=+\tfrac{d}{\sqrt2}(\Omega_1-i\Omega_2)=v_{-1}$.

[(b) $L_3$ and ladder] Compute the polynomial actions with $D_1=x_2\partial_3-x_3\partial_2$, $D_2=x_3\partial_1-x_1\partial_3$, $D_3=x_1\partial_2-x_2\partial_1$ and [F1]: $D_3(\Omega_1\pm i\Omega_2)=\pm i(\Omega_1\pm i\Omega_2)$ (since $D_3\Omega_1=-\Omega_2$, $D_3\Omega_2=\Omega_1$), hence $L_3(\Omega_1\pm i\Omega_2)=\pm\hbar(\Omega_1\pm i\Omega_2)$ and, after the normalisation $v_{\pm1}=\mp\frac{d}{\sqrt2}(\Omega_1\pm i\Omega_2)$, $L_3v_1=\hbar v_1$, $L_3v_{-1}=-\hbar v_{-1}$, and $L_3v_0=0$; further $(D_1+iD_2)(\Omega_1+i\Omega_2)=0$, $(D_1+iD_2)\Omega_3=-i(\Omega_1+i\Omega_2)$, $(D_1+iD_2)(\Omega_1-i\Omega_2)=2i\Omega_3$, so $L_+=-i\hbar(D_1+iD_2)$ satisfies $L_+v_1=0$, $L_+v_0=-i\hbar\,d\,(-i(\Omega_1+i\Omega_2))=-\hbar d(\Omega_1+i\Omega_2)=\sqrt2\hbar v_1$, and $L_+v_{-1}=-i\hbar\,d\,\tfrac{2i}{\sqrt2}\Omega_3=\sqrt2\hbar\,d\,\Omega_3=\sqrt2\hbar v_0$; the relations for $L_-|_{V_1}=(L_+|_{V_1})^*$ follow by the finite-block adjunction of [F1].

[(b) commutators on the core] With the same operators, $L_1x_1=0$, $L_1x_2=i\hbar x_3$, $L_1x_3=-i\hbar x_2$; $L_2x_1=-i\hbar x_3$, $L_2x_2=0$, $L_2x_3=i\hbar x_1$; $L_3x_1=i\hbar x_2$, $L_3x_2=-i\hbar x_1$, $L_3x_3=0$. Evaluating $L_1L_2-L_2L_1$ on $x_1,x_2,x_3$: since $L_2x_1=-i\hbar x_3$ and $L_1x_1=0$ one has $L_1L_2x_1=-i\hbar\,L_1x_3=-\hbar^2x_2$ and $L_2L_1x_1=0$, so $[L_1,L_2]x_1=-\hbar^2x_2=i\hbar(i\hbar x_2)=i\hbar L_3x_1$; $[L_1,L_2]x_2=+\hbar^2x_1=i\hbar L_3x_2$; and $[L_1,L_2]x_3=0=i\hbar L_3x_3$. Hence $[L_1,L_2]=i\hbar L_3$ on $V_1$, and cyclically for the other two pairs, consistent with [F1]. Likewise, squaring the displayed actions: $L_1^2x_1=0$, $L_2^2x_1=\hbar^2x_1$, $L_3^2x_1=\hbar^2x_1$; $L_1^2x_2=i\hbar\,L_1x_3=\hbar^2x_2$, $L_2^2x_2=0$, $L_3^2x_2=\hbar^2x_2$; $L_1^2x_3=\hbar^2x_3$, $L_2^2x_3=\hbar^2x_3$, $L_3^2x_3=0$; in each case the sum is $2\hbar^2x_i$, so $L_1^2+L_2^2+L_3^2=2\hbar^2\,\mathrm{id}$ on $V_1$, which equals $\hbar^2A|_{V_1}$ by [F4]. Alternatively the sum identity follows from the ladder relations of step 2.1 via $L_1^2+L_2^2=\tfrac12(L_+L_-+L_-L_+)$ and $L_1^2+L_2^2+L_3^2=2\hbar^2$ on each $v_m$.

[(c) spin-one equivalence] By steps 1.1 and 2.1 the assignment $e_m\mapsto v_m$ matches the spin-one relations of [F5]: $J_ze_m=me_m$ with $L_3v_m=\hbar mv_m$, and $J_+e_1=0$, $J_+e_0=\sqrt2e_1$, $J_+e_{-1}=\sqrt2e_0$ with $L_+v_1=0$, $L_+v_0=\sqrt2\hbar v_1$, $L_+v_{-1}=\sqrt2\hbar v_0$; since both bases are orthonormal and $L_x=\tfrac12(L_++L_-)$, $L_y=\tfrac1{2i}(L_+-L_-)$ mirror $J_x,J_y$, the assignment is a unitary isomorphism carrying $J_i$ to $\hbar^{-1}L_i$ for $i=x,y,z$. The last assertion is step 3.1 with [F4].
